title: Humans: A Monstrous History
description:
Surekha Davies's Humans: A Monstrous History reads the history of monster-making as a history of who gets to count as normal.

Davies traces how people have defined the human in relation to everything from apes to zombies, and how race, gender and nations were invented along the way. Her examples run from ancient gods and Frankenstein's monster to E.T. and generative AI. Her argument is that monster-making is about control. The University of California Press published it in February 2025 as a 336-page hardcover with ten color plates and forty black-and-white figures.

Davies is a British historian of science, art and ideas. Her first book, Renaissance Ethnography and the Invention of the Human, won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize and the Roland H. Bainton Prize. She has written essays and reviews for the Times Literary Supplement, Nature, Science and Aeon.
tags: History, Monsters, History of Science, Race and Identity, Anthropology

title: Harold's End
description:
JT LeRoy's Harold's End is a short, illustrated novella about a San Francisco street hustler, an older man, and a snail.

The narrator is Oliver, a youth on Polk Street feeding a heroin habit, who is taken in by a man named Larry. Larry provides shelter and drugs and takes an interest in Oliver's pet snail, Harold. The Last Gasp edition runs to 99 pages and is illustrated with eight watercolor paintings by the Australian artist Cherry Hood, each based on the story's character descriptions. Dave Eggers contributes an introduction. Last Gasp also issued signed copies, signed by LeRoy and Hood.

LeRoy's earlier books, Sarah and The Heart Is Deceitful Above All Things, were both international bestsellers, according to Last Gasp. Hood's watercolor of a boy holding a snail in a cup appears in miniature on the black cloth cover.

title: Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea
description:
Charles Seife's Zero is a popular history of one number and the arguments it has set off in mathematics, philosophy, religion and physics.

Seife follows zero from its birth as an Eastern philosophical concept to its struggle for acceptance in Europe and its rise in the West. Along the way he covers the thinkers who tried to understand it, from Pythagoras and Newton to Heisenberg, and the clashes that pitted East against West and faith against reason. The book closes on zero in black holes, the Big Bang and the search for a theory of everything. This Penguin paperback is 256 pages.

Seife is a science journalist and a professor of journalism at New York University. Zero won the PEN/Martha Albrand Award for first nonfiction and was a New York Times Notable Book. His later books include Proofiness. He has written for the New York Times, Wired, New Scientist, Science, Scientific American and The Economist.
tags: Mathematics, History of Science, Philosophy, Physics, Popular Science
notes: Penguin paperback, September 2000. Other editions: Viking hardcover (ISBN 9780670884575), Souvenir Press paperback (ISBN 9780285635944). Identified from a spine photograph; edition not checked against the copy.

title: Paris, Capital of Modernity
description:
A collection of David Harvey's essays on Second Empire Paris, read as the place where nineteenth-century capitalist modernity took shape.

The book is arranged in three parts: Representations, Materializations and a Coda. Early chapters take up the myths of modernity and the body politic. The long middle section follows the city through space relations, credit and finance, rent, the state, labor, women's work, consumerism and spectacle on the boulevards. It reads the work of Balzac, Baudelaire and Zola alongside this material, and closes with the building of the Sacré-Coeur basilica. The volume is heavily illustrated and includes drawings, portraits and cartoons by Daumier.

Harvey is a British-American geographer and Marxist theorist, Distinguished Professor at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York, and long associated with urban political economy and the idea of the right to the city. Here his usual economic analysis is applied to a single city and a single period, with literature and caricature as evidence.
tags: Paris, Urban History, Marxism, Modernity, Second Empire, Cultural Geography

title: The Catwalk Cats
description:
A book of photographs and drawings in which two fashion-world figures portray their household of cats.

Grace Coddington and Didier Malige lived together for more than twenty years with a group of cats, and the book records that household through Malige's photographs and Coddington's drawings. The cats are named and characterised one by one, among them Henri, a catnip-addicted surfer, his sister Coco, and the Persian Bart. Coddington and Malige tell their working and private lives through what the cats see. Sally Singer wrote the introduction and Michael Roberts is credited as editor. It was published in 2006 by Edition 7L, the Steidl imprint.

Coddington is a Welsh former model and former creative director at large of American Vogue, known for large, elaborate and dramatic photographic shoots. Malige is a French hairstylist raised in Paris.

title: Paris versus New York: A Tally of Two Cities
description:
A book of paired graphic illustrations that set Paris against New York, one detail at a time, from a blog the author began while living in New York.

Each spread sets a small image and a short tagline from one city against its counterpart in the other, in graphic form. The book grew out of an online travel journal that Vahram Muratyan started in 2010 during a long stay in New York, written from the point of view of a Parisian wandering the city. The Penguin Books edition appeared in January 2012 and runs to 224 pages. A French edition was published by 10-18, and a later Penguin title, Paris Versus New York: The Complete Series of Two Cities, is listed under another ISBN.

Muratyan is a French visual storyteller and art director. After the blog drew wide attention he showed the series in print at colette in Paris and at The Standard in New York.

title: Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography
description:
Benjamin Franklin's account of his own life, written in four installments over nearly twenty years and left unfinished at his death, is among the best-known life stories in American letters.

The Autobiography begins as a letter to his son William, written in England in 1771. It covers his boyhood in Boston, his apprenticeship to his brother James, and his move to Philadelphia. Franklin resumed it in Paris in 1784, adding his plan for moral perfection through thirteen virtues. Further sections, written in 1788 and in the last months of his life, cover his almanac, his electrical experiments, and his mission to London for the Pennsylvania Assembly. It first appeared in French in 1791. This is the Everyman's Library edition, no. 316, from J.M. Dent & Sons of London with E.P. Dutton in New York.

Franklin (1706 to 1790) was a printer, the author of Poor Richard's Almanack, and a scientist. He was the first American ambassador to France and signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. Everyman's Library was founded in 1906 by J.M. Dent, with Ernest Rhys as editor, to put a wide collection of world literature in affordable pocket-sized hardcovers.

title: No Way Back 002: Better Ways Forward Through Music and Subculture Stories, 1979–1997
contributors: Steven Harvey (Original contributor (reprinted)); Steve Eichner (Original contributor (reprinted)); Sheryl Garratt (Original contributor (reprinted)); Jon Savage (Original contributor (reprinted)); Paul Morley (Original contributor (reprinted)); Eddie Otchere (Original contributor (reprinted)); Kodwo Eshun (Original contributor (reprinted))
description:
No Way Back 002 is the second issue of a printed magazine that reprints period journalism and photography on music, clubs and subculture from 1979 to 1997.

The issue gathers pieces from The Face, i-D, Time Out, Village Voice, Rolling Stone, Mixmag, The Observer and David Toop's Collusion. It also reproduces photographs and covers and spreads from the original titles. Steven Harvey's 1983 Collusion feature covers the New York disco underground. Steve Eichner photographed the club kids at The Limelight, Palladium, Tunnel and Club USA. Sheryl Garratt reported from Chicago for The Face in 1986, Jon Savage spent a night at Jive Turkey in Sheffield, and Kodwo Eshun wrote on jungle for i-D in 1994, with jungle images from Eddie Otchere. The editors add notes and playlists. It runs 208 pages at 165 × 240 mm and went on sale in April 2026.

The first issue, NWB001, covered 1977 to 1989. This one moves the span to 1979–1997 and keeps the focus on moments in dance music, hip-hop and pop, with parallel shifts in art, design and fashion. The publisher describes the material as culture recorded in the moment, before later interpretation settled over it. The issue carries ISSN 2977-8530 and no ISBN.

title: Top Shelf
description:
Top Shelf is a one-off limited-edition publication from The World of Interiors devoted to sex and erotica in design, issued alongside the magazine's body-themed September 2026 issue.

The 76-page volume at 165 × 222 mm sets images against four essays. The essays take up a museum's collection of sexually explicit objects, the use of the human body in decoration and design, the erotics of renovation, and the sexually explicit furniture associated with Catherine the Great. The pictures run from 19th-century brothel architecture to medieval pilgrim badges, contemporary film concept art and contested sculpture. The editors frame the project around the tension between revelation and concealment in domestic space, which is the parent magazine's long-standing subject.

The World of Interiors is a London magazine owned by Condé Nast. Emily Tobin is editor-in-chief and Ben Weaver is art director. The dating app Feeld sponsored Top Shelf, and the launch was held at Shreeji News in London. The cover uses an engraved sheet of nude figures in framed vignettes under the magazine's name.

title: Subliminal: How Your Unconscious Mind Rules Your Behavior
description:
Subliminal is a popular account of cognitive and social psychology by the physicist Leonard Mlodinow, arguing that much of what drives perception, memory and judgment happens outside conscious awareness.

Pantheon published the hardcover in 2012, at 260 pages. The chapters move from the brain's two tiers and the new science of the unconscious to how the senses and the mind together build a picture of reality, how memory works and fails, and how people read one another in social life. The book won the 2013 PEN/E.O. Wilson Literary Science Writing Award, and Vintage issued a 272-page paperback in February 2013.

Mlodinow holds a PhD in theoretical physics from UC Berkeley and taught at Caltech. He co-wrote The Grand Design and A Briefer History of Time with Stephen Hawking, and the cover of this book names his earlier bestseller The Drunkard's Walk. Subliminal applies the same explanatory habit to psychology.

title: The Historical Atlas of New York City: A Visual Celebration of 400 Years of New York City's History
description:
A historical atlas of New York City built from maps, drawings and charts, tracing the city's growth across nearly 400 years.

Eric Homberger's text runs from early Native American culture to the present, with Alice Hudson credited as cartographic consultant. The first edition appeared from Henry Holt in 1994 at 192 pages. This revised and updated edition was issued in 2005 by Holt Paperbacks at 208 pages, and its cover carries a photograph of the Flatiron Building.

Homberger is credited as sole author of both editions, and the 1994 hardcover was part of the Henry Holt Reference Book series.

title: The Big U
description:
The Big U is Neal Stephenson's first novel, a campus satire about a university that fills a single building and slowly comes apart.

The setting is the fictitious American Megaversity, a central complex ringed by eight towers of student housing that makes an enclosed universe of its own. The campus parallels Boston University, and its dormitories resemble Warren Towers. The story follows a series of escalating events that end with a full-scale civil war raging across the campus. Vintage Books published it in the United States in 1984 as a 307-page paperback original, with the cover line "The lowest form of higher education."

The book was out of print by the time Snow Crash made Stephenson famous, and he later allowed it to be reissued. It comes four years before Zodiac (1988) and eight before Snow Crash (1992).
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Satire, Campus Novel, Debut Novel
notes: First edition: Vintage Books trade paperback original, 1984. Stephenson's first novel.

title: Zodiac
description:
Zodiac is Neal Stephenson's second novel, an eco-thriller about a chemist who goes after industrial polluters in Boston Harbor.

Sangamon Taylor works for GEE, a fictional environmental group, and uncovers a conspiracy involving Basco Industries, a fictional corporation that produced Agent Orange and is now experimenting with genetic engineering to create microbes that make chemicals. When Taylor interferes with Basco's plans, the company frames him as a terrorist to discredit him. The action centers on Boston Harbor, and many late events take place on Spectacle Island, which was almost entirely garbage when the book appeared. Atlantic Monthly Press issued it in 1988 as a 283-page trade paperback original with cover art by Steve Carver.

Zodiac follows the campus satire The Big U (1984) and precedes Snow Crash (1992), the book that made Stephenson's reputation.
tags: Fiction, Thriller, Eco-Thriller, Environment, Boston
notes: First edition: Atlantic Monthly Press trade paperback original, 1988, 283 pages, subtitled The Eco-Thriller. Stephenson's second novel. The first hardcover appeared only in 2010 (Subterranean Press).

title: Snow Crash
description:
Snow Crash is Neal Stephenson's 1992 cyberpunk novel about a hacker, a virtual world, and a digital narcotic that harms people outside it.

Hiro Protagonist is a freelance hacker and a pizza delivery driver for the Mafia. He partners with Y.T., a skateboard courier, and the two gather intelligence to sell to the CIC, a for-profit organization that grew out of a merger of the CIA and the Library of Congress. A datafile called Snow Crash, offered in the Metaverse, is linked to a drug, and a friend's exposure to it causes brain damage in the real world. The setting is a future America after a worldwide economic collapse, where Los Angeles is no longer part of the United States and franchise-run quasi-national entities govern large areas. Bantam published it in hardcover in 1992. It was nominated for the 1993 British Science Fiction Award and the 1994 Arthur C. Clarke Award, and appears on Time's list of the 100 best English-language novels since 1923.

It is Stephenson's third novel, after The Big U and Zodiac, and the book that made him famous. Interface and The Diamond Age followed within three years.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Cyberpunk, Virtual Reality, Dystopia
notes: First edition: Bantam Books hardcover, 1992 (Bantam Spectra imprint).

title: Interface
description:
Interface is a political thriller that Neal Stephenson wrote with J. Frederick George, first published under their joint pseudonym Stephen Bury.

The story is set in the then-future year of 1996. A coalition of businesses called the Network plans to manipulate a candidate for the US presidency through a computer biochip implanted in his brain. After Illinois governor William Cozzano suffers a stroke, the Network has the chip put in so that he can run. Because the chip is linked to public opinion polls, it can change what he says or does according to public sentiment. Eleanor Richmond, an unemployed woman living in a trailer park, becomes a vice presidential candidate after the Network selects her. Bantam published it on 1 April 1994 as a 583-page paperback.

It appeared between Snow Crash (1992) and The Diamond Age (1995). Reprints credit Stephenson and George by name, and J. Frederick George is itself a pseudonym of George Jewsbury.
tags: Fiction, Thriller, Political Thriller, Pseudonymous Work, Technology
notes: First edition: Bantam Books trade paperback original, 1 April 1994, published as by Stephen Bury, the joint pseudonym of Neal Stephenson and J. Frederick George. Later printings credit Stephenson and George.

title: The Diamond Age
description:
The Diamond Age is a 1995 science fiction novel about a girl, a stolen interactive book, and a society reorganized around nanotechnology.

Nell is a thete, a person without a phyle, growing up in the Leased Territories, a slum on the artificial island of New Chusan near Shanghai. She comes into possession of the Young Lady's Illustrated Primer, an interactive book commissioned for another girl. Its designer, John Percival Hackworth, made an unauthorized copy for his own daughter, and the two storylines intersect. The setting is the twenty-second century, where molecular nanotechnology is everywhere and cultural groups called phyles have replaced nation-states. Bantam Spectra published it in hardcover in February 1995. It won the 1996 Hugo Award for Best Novel and the 1996 Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel.

It followed Snow Crash (1992) and Interface (1994), and preceded Cryptonomicon (1999).
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Nanotechnology, Coming-of-Age, Hugo Award
notes: First edition: Bantam Spectra hardcover, February 1995, 455 pages. Full title on the jacket is The Diamond Age, or A Young Lady's Illustrated Primer. Winner of the 1996 Hugo and Locus awards.

title: Cryptonomicon
description:
Cryptonomicon is a 1999 novel that cuts between Second World War codebreaking and the internet boom of the late 1990s.

In 1942, Lawrence Pritchard Waterhouse, a US Navy code breaker, joins a secret Anglo-American unit that stages events to hide the fact that the Allies have cracked the German Enigma code. Marine Bobby Shaftoe carries out its operations, while Japanese soldiers, among them the mining engineer Goto Dengo, build a mountain bunker in the Philippines. In the late 1990s, Randy Waterhouse and Avi Halaby start a company that sends video messages to Filipino migrants, and their parent firm funds a data haven in the fictional Sultanate of Kinakuta. Avon published it in hardcover in 1999. It won the 2000 Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel and was nominated for the Hugo and Arthur C. Clarke awards that year.

The Baroque Cycle, set in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, supplies part of its backstory with ancestors of several characters, and Enoch Root appears in both works. Stephenson's 2019 novel Fall; or, Dodge in Hell later placed these books in the same universe as Reamde.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Cryptography, World War II, Technology
notes: First edition: Avon hardcover, 1999, 918 pages. Stephenson's later Baroque Cycle supplies part of the backstory to this novel.

title: Quicksilver
description:
Quicksilver is the first volume of Neal Stephenson's Baroque Cycle, a historical novel set mainly between the 1660 Restoration and the 1688 Glorious Revolution.

A frame story opens in Massachusetts in late 1713, when Enoch Root arrives in Boston with a summons for Daniel Waterhouse from Princess Caroline. She wants Daniel to return to England and try to mend the feud between Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz. Flashbacks follow Daniel's life from 1661 to 1673, including his friendship with Newton at Cambridge and his work with Robert Hooke and John Wilkins, while the vagabond Jack Shaftoe and Eliza, a former harem member, cross Europe after the Battle of Vienna. The volume holds three books: Quicksilver, The King of the Vagabonds and Odalisque. William Morrow published it in hardcover in 2003, and it won the 2004 Arthur C. Clarke Award.

The cycle runs to three volumes and eight books and supplies part of the backstory to Cryptonomicon (1999), where Enoch Root also appears.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Science Fiction, The Baroque Cycle, Scientific Revolution
notes: First edition: William Morrow hardcover, 23 September 2003. Volume One of The Baroque Cycle (Quicksilver, The Confusion, The System of the World). Contains three books: Quicksilver, King of the Vagabonds, Odalisque. Winner of the 2004 Arthur C. Clarke Award.

title: The Confusion
description:
The Confusion is the second volume of the Baroque Cycle, built from two novels that alternate section by section: Bonanza and The Juncto.

It continues directly from Quicksilver with no time jump and moves across Europe, the Mediterranean, India, the Philippines, Japan, and Mexico. Bonanza follows Jack Shaftoe, who wakes from a long blackout as a former galley slave and joins fellow slaves in seizing a Spanish treasure ship that turns out to carry gold rather than silver. The Juncto follows Eliza, who loses her fortune to French demands and later works against the French invasion of England, and Bob Shaftoe, who serves in William III's Irish campaign. Its second half turns to Daniel Waterhouse, Newton and Leibniz, and to the founding of the Bank of England and the reform of the English currency. William Morrow published the 815-page hardcover in April 2004.

It is the middle of three volumes, between Quicksilver (2003) and The System of the World, and part of the backstory to Cryptonomicon (1999).
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Adventure, The Baroque Cycle, Scientific Revolution
notes: First edition: William Morrow hardcover, April 2004, 815 pages. Volume Two of The Baroque Cycle, made of two books, Bonanza and The Juncto, printed in alternating sections.

title: The System of the World
description:
The System of the World closes the Baroque Cycle, Neal Stephenson's historical fiction about the birth of modern science and finance.

The novel opens with Daniel Waterhouse returning to England from Boston to settle the quarrel between Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz over who invented calculus. An assassination attempt with a time bomb follows him, and Jack Shaftoe, working as a coiner, plots a heist at the Tower of London. Eliza meanwhile supports Princess Caroline of Hanover as the succession to Queen Anne is contested. Newton's work at the Mint and the Trial of the Pyx run through the plot. The title alludes to the third volume of Newton's Principia. William Morrow published it in September 2004, and it won the Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel and the Prometheus Award in 2005. It was also shortlisted for the Arthur C. Clarke Award.

It follows The Confusion and ends a project that ran across three books. Stephenson later turned to fiction set on another planet in Anathem and in the present day in Reamde.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Historical Fiction, The Baroque Cycle, Isaac Newton, Early Modern England
notes: First hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2004). The Baroque Cycle, volume three; preceded by The Confusion.

title: Anathem
description:
Anathem is a novel of ideas that sets a science-fiction first-contact story inside a world of cloistered philosophers and mathematicians.

It takes place on the fictional planet Arbre, where intellectuals long ago withdrew into monastic communities called concents to protect their work from the collapse of society. These avout are barred from most advanced technology and watched by an Inquisition. The narrator, Fraa Erasmas, lives at the Concent of Saunt Edhar. His teacher Orolo spots an alien spacecraft in orbit and is banished, in the rite that gives the book its title, for using a forbidden video camera to observe it. The story then follows Erasmas out of the concent and into a journey toward the pole and a council of avout and secular powers. Its themes include the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics and the debate between Platonic realism and nominalism. William Morrow published the 937-page hardcover on September 9, 2008, and it won the Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel in 2009.

Anathem was Stephenson's first novel after the Baroque Cycle, which ended four years earlier. Reamde followed in 2011.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Philosophy, Quantum Mechanics, Monasticism, First Contact
notes: First hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2008). Winner of the 2009 Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel.

title: Reamde
description:
Reamde is a present-day thriller that follows a kidnapping across three continents and runs it through the economy of an online fantasy game.

Zula Forthrast, an adopted Eritrean, works for her uncle Richard "Dodge" Forthrast at Corporation 9592, the company behind the MMORPG T'Rain. When her boyfriend sells a database of stolen credit card numbers, a T'Rain-based ransomware virus ruins the data and the Russian mob comes after the people who wrote it. The hunt leads to Xiamen, China, where Zula is taken hostage by an Islamist cell and carried toward North America while family, hired security and intelligence agents try to find her. The book covers gold farming, social networking and the methods of organized crime. William Morrow published the 1044-page hardcover in September 2011.

Where Anathem invents a planet and the Baroque Cycle reaches back to the seventeenth century, Reamde is set in the contemporary world. Stephenson returned to the Forthrast family in Fall; or, Dodge in Hell (2019).
tags: Fiction, Thriller, Science Fiction, Online Games, Organized Crime, Terrorism
notes: First hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2011).

title: The Mongoliad: Book One
contributors: Greg Bear (Co-author); Erik Bear (Co-author); Joseph Brassey (Co-author); Nicole Galland (Co-author); Cooper Moo (Co-author); Mark Teppo (Co-author)
description:
The Mongoliad: Book One is the first print volume of a collaborative adventure novel that began as a serialized app and web project.

The Subutai Corporation, which Stephenson helped found, serialized the story online and through iOS and Android apps from September 2010 to January 2012. The idea began with Stephenson's dissatisfaction with the early modern swordfighting he had written in the Baroque Cycle, which led him to gather students of historical European martial arts. 47North issued the restructured text in print on April 24, 2012, credited to Stephenson, Greg Bear, Erik Bear, Joseph Brassey, Nicole Galland (as E.D. deBirmingham), Cooper Moo and Mark Teppo. The series is set in the Foreworld universe in 1241, as Mongol armies move on Europe under the successors of Genghis Khan. This paperback runs about 440 pages.

Stephenson is the chairman of Subutai and one of several authors here, which sets the book apart from his solo novels such as Anathem. It is volume one of three in the first Mongoliad sequence.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Adventure, Foreworld Saga, The Mongoliad Cycle, Mongol Empire, Medieval Europe
notes: First print edition (47North, 2012), paperback original. Volume one of The Mongoliad Cycle (the Foreworld Saga).

title: The Mongoliad: Book Two
contributors: Greg Bear (Co-author); Erik Bear (Co-author); Joseph Brassey (Co-author); Nicole Galland (Co-author); Cooper Moo (Co-author); Mark Teppo (Co-author)
description:
The Mongoliad: Book Two continues the Foreworld adventure in the middle volume of the first Mongoliad trilogy.

47North published it in September 2012, five months after Book One, with the same credited team: Stephenson, Greg Bear, Erik Bear, Joseph Brassey, Nicole Galland (writing as E.D. deBirmingham), Cooper Moo and Mark Teppo. The story keeps to the year 1241 and runs several lines at once. The narrative follows a small group of fighters and mystics in medieval Europe and describes the Eurasian steppe and the court of Ögedei Khan, while a separate thread in Rome follows a papal conclave in detail. Orders of knights formed during the Crusades, including the Teutonic Order and the Hospitallers, are among the groups drawn into the narrative.

The series began as an app-based serial and was restructured for print. Book Two sits between the opening volume and Book Three, which followed in 2013.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Adventure, Foreworld Saga, The Mongoliad Cycle, Mongol Empire, Papal Conclave
notes: First print edition (47North, 2012), paperback original. Volume two of The Mongoliad Cycle (the Foreworld Saga).

title: The Mongoliad: Book Three
contributors: Greg Bear (Co-author); Erik Bear (Co-author); Joseph Brassey (Co-author); Nicole Galland (Co-author); Cooper Moo (Co-author); Mark Teppo (Co-author)
description:
The Mongoliad: Book Three is the last volume of the first Mongoliad trilogy and the final book to carry Stephenson's name before the series moved to other authors.

47North published the paperback in February 2013. It is credited to Stephenson, Greg Bear, Erik Bear, Joseph Brassey, Nicole Galland, Cooper Moo and Mark Teppo, and runs 698 pages. The cycle is set in 1241 during the Mongol invasion of Europe, with parallel lines in Rome, Poland, Russia, and Central Asia. The later books of the series draw in Holy Grail legend and Norse mythology. Mongol events described in the books include the death of Ögedei Khan and the recall of the khans to choose a successor.

Katabasis, Book Four of the Foreworld Saga, appeared in October 2013 and was the first Foreworld novel not co-authored by Stephenson. Book Three therefore closes his own part in the print cycle.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Adventure, Foreworld Saga, The Mongoliad Cycle, Mongol Empire, Medieval Europe
notes: First print edition (47North, 2013), paperback original. Volume three of The Mongoliad Cycle (the Foreworld Saga).

title: Seveneves
description:
Seveneves is a hard science fiction novel about what humanity does when it has two years to prepare for the end of Earth.

An unknown agent shatters the Moon, and the astronomer Doc Dubois Harris calculates that the fragments will rain down in what he calls the Hard Rain, making Earth uninhabitable for thousands of years. The world's governments launch a swarm of small habitats, the Cloud Ark, around the International Space Station. Part Two follows the decimated survivors through violence, loss, and a journey to the exposed iron core of the Moon. Part Three jumps five thousand years ahead, to a civilization of three billion people living in a ring around the Earth. William Morrow published the hardcover on May 19, 2015, at 880 pages.

Seveneves follows Reamde, published four years earlier, and returns from that present-day thriller to the speculative ground of Anathem.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Hard Science Fiction, Space Exploration, Apocalyptic Fiction, Genetics
notes: First hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2015).

title: The Rise and Fall of D.O.D.O.
description:
The Rise and Fall of D.O.D.O. is a time-travel novel by Neal Stephenson and Nicole Galland, built around a secret U.S. government agency that tries to change history through magic.

The agency is the Department of Diachronic Operations, which gives the book its title. The story is set mainly in the present-day United States, and the agency sends its operatives into historical periods that include London in 1601, Constantinople in 1203 and 1204, and London in 1851. William Morrow published the hardcover on June 13, 2017, at 768 pages, and it entered the New York Times hardcover fiction list at number 11.

Stephenson and Galland had already written together on The Mongoliad, the shared-authorship serial published in three volumes in 2012 and 2013. Stephenson returned to solo novels with Fall; or, Dodge in Hell (2019).
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Fantasy, Time Travel, Collaboration
notes: First US hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2017), written with Nicole Galland. Book one of the D.O.D.O. series.

title: Fall; or, Dodge in Hell
description:
Fall; or, Dodge in Hell is a novel about what follows when a dead man's mind is kept as data and starts building a world.

Richard "Dodge" Forthrast, a billionaire, is declared brain-dead. Under his will his body is cryonically preserved and his brain is destructively scanned, with the connectome saved digitally. Years later his grandniece Sophia runs the connectome as a senior-thesis experiment, and it builds a virtual world that comes to resemble a medieval fantasy setting. The struggle over that world pits Dodge against El, a dying billionaire who takes control of it and sets up a religion around himself. William Morrow published the hardcover on June 4, 2019.

Dodge first appeared in Reamde (2011), the novel that precedes this one. Both books share a fictional universe with Cryptonomicon and The Baroque Cycle, which ties the novel back to the earlier strand of Stephenson's fiction.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Virtual Reality, Cryonics, Reamde Universe
notes: First US hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2019).

title: Atmosphaera Incognita
description:
Atmosphaera Incognita is a short novella about building a tower 20 kilometers high toward outer space, issued by Subterranean Press as an illustrated hardcover.

The story follows the multi-year construction of the tower, a modern take on the Tower of Babel legend, and concentrates on the perseverance, planning, and technology the project demands. It also describes the atmosphere itself, the layer between the planet and space, with its beauties and hazards. Patrick Arrasmith made the dust jacket and the interior illustrations. Subterranean lists the book at 104 pages, and Booklist describes the story as 93 pages.

According to Publishers Weekly, quoted on the publisher's page, Stephenson wrote the piece in 2013 for Hieroglyph, an idea-incubation project. It is a short work in a bibliography of long novels, set beside books such as Termination Shock at 720 pages.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Novella, Illustrated Book, Hieroglyph, Space Tower
notes: First edition, trade hardcover (Subterranean Press, 2019), illustrated by Patrick Arrasmith. The title is printed as Atmosphæra Incognita.

title: Termination Shock
description:
Termination Shock is a near-future novel about one billionaire's attempt to cool the planet and the governments forced to respond.

T.R. Schmidt, a Texas oil-industry billionaire, launches a solar geoengineering scheme that fires sulfur into the stratosphere to mimic a volcanic eruption. The effects are uneven. Some low-lying areas benefit while Punjab faces drought, and the title refers to the sudden rapid warming that would follow if the scheme were stopped abruptly. The settings include the Texas-Mexico border, the Netherlands, Venice, the Maldives, Punjab, and the China-India border. The characters include Queen Frederika of the Netherlands, Rufus Grant, a part-Comanche exterminator of feral hogs, and Deep "Laks" Singh, a Punjab-Canadian Sikh. William Morrow published the hardcover on November 16, 2021, at 720 pages.

It is the novel Stephenson published between Fall; or, Dodge in Hell (2019) and Polostan (2024), the first volume of his Bomb Light series.
tags: Fiction, Science Fiction, Climate Change, Geoengineering, Near Future
notes: First US hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2021).

title: Polostan
description:
Polostan is the first volume of Bomb Light, a planned historical-fiction series about the dawn of the Atomic Age.

The novel is set in the Soviet Union and the United States in 1933 and 1934. It follows Dawn Rae's early life as she moves between the two countries and is groomed as a spy for the organization that later became the KGB. Figures and events of the decade appear along the way, among them George S. Patton, Lavrentiy Beria, and the Century of Progress. William Morrow published the hardcover on October 15, 2024.

Where Termination Shock (2021) looked ahead to a near-future climate crisis, Polostan looks back to the 1930s. The series continues with D: Heavy Water, published in October 2026 as the second Bomb Light volume.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Espionage, Bomb Light, Soviet Union, Atomic Age
notes: First US hardcover edition (William Morrow, 2024). Volume one of the Bomb Light series.

title: D: Heavy Water
description:
D: Heavy Water is the second volume of Neal Stephenson's Bomb Light series, an espionage novel about the race to secure the only supply of heavy water before it falls to the Nazis.

Owen Crisp-Upjohn, a British journalist, is sent to Moscow in 1934. His assignment turns into espionage when he joins an eccentric aristocrat, the Earl of Suffolk, and Aurora, a woman with a Soviet intelligence past. Their mission is to secure the world's only supply of deuterium. The story moves from London to Barcelona during the Spanish Civil War, then to Soviet airfields and occupied Norway. William Morrow published the hardcover on October 13, 2026, at 448 pages.

The first volume, Polostan (2024), is set in 1933 and 1934, and this book begins in Moscow in 1934. Both are historical novels, a turn from the near-future setting of Termination Shock.
tags: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Espionage, Bomb Light, World War II, Heavy Water
notes: First US hardcover edition (William Morrow, October 2026). Volume two of the Bomb Light series; Polostan is volume one.
